newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish police discover suspected Loyalist bomb.
newsitem.headline: Irish police discover suspected Loyalist bomb.

text.p: Army experts on Sunday carried out a controlled explosion on a suspected bomb which was thought planted by Northern Ireland Protestant extremists.
Irish police said they received a coded warning about a package left in an alley in the town of Dundalk, some five miles (eight km) from the border with British-ruled Northern Ireland.
The caller said he represented a "Loyalist Paramilitary Organisation" but did not say which of Northern Ireland's Loyalist organisations he meant.
All are supposed to be observing a truce since October 1994 as part of Northern Ireland's slow-moving peace process.

Loyalists have waged a decades-long guerrilla war against Irish and Roman Catholic targets to keep Northern Ireland British and want the Irish government to drop a constitutional claim to the province.
The device was planted days before Ireland's June 6 election in a major town on the main Belfast-to-Dublin road.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA), which is fighting a rival guerrilla war to end British rule in Northern Ireland, disrupted traffic and daily life during Britain's April election campaign with a series of bomb warnings, both hoax and real.
Local media reports said the device found on Sunday appeared similar to one used in an attack on the offices of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing in March.
They said a detonator and timer appeared to have been used. The remains of the package was taken to Dublin police forensic experts.
Loyalists, who trace their name to their allegiance to Britain, are officially observing a ceasefire which they called to match an IRA truce in October 1994.
But a spate of recent attacks has been blamed by police on a variety of Loyalist groupings and are seen as reprisals for Irish republican violence.

This include the fatal shooting of an off-duty policeman by the Irish National Liberation Army, an IRA splinter group which has never formally called a ceasefire. The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year.

The IRA has not struck in Northern Ireland itself for several weeks, prompting speculation that the guerrillas are observing an unofficial truce while Sinn Fein holds exploratory talks with officials serving Britain's new Labour government.
Sinn Fein is barred from Northern Ireland's peace talks grouping Irish nationalists and pro-British Unionists until its guerrilla backers end their war against British rule.
